title: Sorting: Insertion Sort
oneLiner: Grow a sorted prefix one element at a time, sliding each new element back to where it belongs.
keyTakeaway: Insertion sort is O(n^2) worst case, same as bubble sort -- but O(n) on already-nearly-sorted input, because it does genuinely useful, permanent work as it goes (the sorted prefix is really done, not just "the biggest value found its spot"). That's why real-world sorts often fall back to insertion sort for small subarrays inside a faster algorithm.
explanation: Treat index 0 as a trivially-sorted prefix of length one. For every next index i, pull out nums[i] and slide it leftward past anything bigger in the sorted prefix, shifting those bigger elements one slot to the right as you go -- then drop nums[i] into the gap it opened up. After processing index i, indices [0..i] are fully sorted. Watch out for the shifting direction: you're moving BIGGER elements right to make room, not moving the new element right -- get that backwards and you'll sort in the wrong order or overwrite data.

starterCode.python:
def insertion_sort(nums):
    # TODO: for each index i from 1, slide nums[i] left past bigger elements
    # in the sorted prefix [0..i-1], shifting them right to make room.
    return nums

visualizationSteps.message: Starting array: [5, 2, 4, 1, 3]. Index 0 is trivially a sorted prefix of length 1.
Take arr[1] = 2. Slide it left past anything bigger in the sorted prefix [0..0].
2 belongs at index 0. Sorted prefix is now [0..1].
Take arr[2] = 4. Slide it left past anything bigger in the sorted prefix [0..1].
4 belongs at index 1. Sorted prefix is now [0..2].
Take arr[3] = 1. Slide it left past anything bigger in the sorted prefix [0..2].
1 belongs at index 0. Sorted prefix is now [0..3].
Take arr[4] = 3. Slide it left past anything bigger in the sorted prefix [0..3].
3 belongs at index 2. Sorted prefix is now [0..4].

complexity.note: Worst case shifts every earlier element for each insert (~n²/2), in place. Nearly-sorted input runs close to O(n).
